say.text: Exam drill: eleven stems, set the way PYQs set them. Read the qualifier word before you tap.
A question says 'modified Brooke' and asks what that wording changes from the classic formula.

choices.label: Adds colloid to the 4 mL Parkland volume
Crystalloid only: 2 mL Ringer lactate per kg per %TBSA
Nothing changes; the 4 mL key still applies
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Colloid feels like part of every named formula, since Brooke and Evans carry it. But classic Parkland gives crystalloid only in its first 24 hours, so colloid is not what the qualifier changes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check each formula's fluids before you name it. Colloid belongs to Brooke and Evans, not to the Parkland volume.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The 4 mL key is the one you have memorised, and PYQs do expect it. But the word 'modified' is in the stem, so reading the qualifier comes before the formula.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but the memorised key ignores the qualifier. Read 'modified' or 'current' first, then pick the formula.

say.text: Brooke carries colloid. Ask what a modified version drops from the classic formula, and which fluid it keeps.
Crystalloid only, 2 mL Ringer lactate per kg per %TBSA. Modified Brooke drops the colloid and starts at 2 mL. The 4 mL figure is the PYQ key for a stem with no qualifier.
Topical burn agents are set as one-line recall. Which agent causes metabolic acidosis?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
It is the default agent in most units, so its name fills every topical question. But its named problem is leucopenia, not acidosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the pair: silver sulfadiazine's side effect is leucopenia.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Silver is the word you recall, and silver agents feel alike. But silver nitrate's side effects are hyponatraemia and black staining, not acidosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the pair: silver nitrate causes hyponatraemia and a black stain.

say.text: Each agent has one side effect you must remember. Match the side effect to the agent, not to the word silver.
Mafenide acetate. It penetrates eschar, and its carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes metabolic acidosis.
Which of these is the antidote for cyanide, not for carbon monoxide?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Oxygen is the first treatment for carbon monoxide, so it feels like the smoke antidote. But oxygen treats carbon monoxide, and cyanide needs its own drug.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two smoke poisons: oxygen is the carbon monoxide treatment.

say.text: That choice is not right.
It is a well-known antidote, so it feels like a general burn-related remedy. But it is the hydrofluoric acid antidote, not a smoke-gas antidote.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie calcium gluconate to its own poison, hydrofluoric acid.

say.text: Match each drug to the poison it was made for. Which poison is the one this question asks about?
Hydroxocobalamin, the cyanide antidote in smoke inhalation, given when cyanide is suspected. Oxygen treats carbon monoxide, and calcium gluconate treats hydrofluoric acid.
A 35-year-old has a burn that wraps the whole chest. He breathes fast, and the ventilator pressures keep climbing. Which burn needs escharotomy now?

choices.label: Circumferential full-thickness chest burn with rising airway pressures
Deep partial-thickness chest burn, blistered and painful
Superficial chest burn over the whole front, ventilating well
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
A deep burn that blisters and hurts feels like the burn that needs cutting. But this burn is partial thickness, so its eschar is not what restricts the chest.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the depth first: escharotomy is for full-thickness skin.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A burn over the whole chest sounds serious, so size seems to justify the cut. But a superficial burn does not restrict ventilation, so there is nothing to release.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so size alone is not the indication; ask whether the skin is constricting breathing.

say.text: Check two things: how deep the skin is, and whether the burn goes all the way round the chest.
The circumferential full-thickness chest burn. Full-thickness eschar that encircles the chest and restricts ventilation needs escharotomy.
Which stress ulcer of the stomach or duodenum appears in the first days after major burns?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Both eponyms sit under 'burns', so the shared word pulls them together. But Marjolin's ulcer is a carcinoma in a chronic scar, not an acute gut ulcer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the site: this ulcer is in the gut, early, not in a scar.

say.text: Ask two things: is the ulcer in the gut or in a scar, and how soon after the burn does it appear?
Curling's ulcer, an acute gastroduodenal stress ulcer after major burns that appears early, so prophylaxis is given from the start.
Same qualifier, now a number. A 50 kg adult has 20% TBSA burned, and the question says 'modified Brooke'. What is the 24-hour Ringer lactate volume?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Four mL times weight times %TBSA is the figure you reach for first. But the stem's 'modified' changes the per-kg figure, so the 4 mL product answers an unqualified stem.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier before you multiply.

say.text: That choice is not right.
1.5 mL is the crystalloid part of the Brooke formula, so the number looks like a Brooke answer. But the modified formula has no colloid and uses its own per-kg figure.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the Brooke crystalloid figure from the modified one.

say.text: Work the numbers in order: weight, then burn size, then the per-kg figure the qualifier selects.
About 2,000 mL in 24 h: 2 mL times 50 kg times 20 of Ringer lactate, with no colloid. The 4 mL key gives 4,000 mL only for an unqualified stem.
A burn to the ear cartilage needs an agent that penetrates the eschar. Which agent, and what do you watch for?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Silver sulfadiazine is the default agent, and leucopenia is the side effect you recalled. But it is broad and painless, not the penetrating agent this cartilage needs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the penetration question comes before the side effect.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Mafenide is the penetrating agent this site needs, so the choice feels right. But leucopenia is silver sulfadiazine's side effect, and mafenide's own problem is different.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the side effect with its own agent before you tap.

say.text: Ask which agent goes deepest into eschar, then pair that agent with its own side effect.
Mafenide, watch for metabolic acidosis. It penetrates eschar, which suits cartilage, and it causes acidosis through carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
What does 100% oxygen actually work on in smoke poisoning?

choices.label: Both smoke poisons, so oxygen covers the smoke
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Cyanide kills at the cell, so oxygen sounds like a cell fix. But oxygen does not clear cyanide's block, and cyanide needs its own antidote.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the mechanisms: cyanide blocks the cell, not the blood.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Both poisons come from the same fire, and oxygen is the first word that comes to mind for smoke. But the two poisons act by different routes, so one treatment does not cover both.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but the two smoke poisons need different treatments.

say.text: Think about what each poison does to the blood, not to the fire.
Carbon monoxide held on haemoglobin. Oxygen speeds its clearance, cutting the half-life from several hours to about one hour.
An old burn scar has a non-healing ulcer with raised, everted edges. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. What is it?

choices.label: Stress ulcer that has moved into the scar
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
It is a burn ulcer that has been around a long time, so the timing feels plausible. But stress ulcers belong to the gut, and a cancer in a scar is a chronic-scar lesion.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the site: a stress ulcer does not move into scar tissue.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Curling's is the burn ulcer you learned first, so the name comes to mind. But Curling's is an acute gut ulcer, while this lesion is a carcinoma in a scar.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the timing: Curling's is early and in the gut.

say.text: Check the biopsy first: which cell type does it show, and where is the lesion?
Marjolin's ulcer, a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic burn scar, usually late. Curling's ulcer is an acute gut stress ulcer.
Which named formula gives 1 mL of colloid per kg per %TBSA in its first 24 hours?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Brooke is the other colloid formula, and its figures look similar. But Brooke has its own colloid ratio, so the figure in this stem does not match it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check each formula's colloid ratio before you name it.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Parkland is the formula most people learn first, and it is the one given in a burn. But classic Parkland gives crystalloid only in its first 24 hours, so it has no colloid ratio.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that Parkland's first 24 hours carry no colloid.

say.text: Two of these formulae include colloid. Compare the colloid figure each one uses.
Evans formula. It gives 1 mL crystalloid and 1 mL colloid per kg per %TBSA, plus dextrose. Parkland has no colloid in the first 24 hours.
Why does a full-thickness circumferential limb burn threaten the limb?

choices.label: Every deep burn forms eschar, so cut it at once
Any circumferential burn needs release, whatever its depth
Inelastic eschar constricts as oedema builds
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Every deep burn does form a crust, and cutting early feels like prevention. But eschar only needs release when it is full thickness and constricting, not whenever a burn is deep.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so depth alone does not justify the cut. Ask whether the eschar is constricting.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A ring of burn sounds like the one that needs the cut. But release is for full-thickness eschar, so a circumferential partial-thickness burn does not need it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the depth decides the cut as well as the ring.

say.text: Think about what happens when a limb swells under skin that cannot stretch.
Inelastic eschar constricts as oedema builds, compressing the distal vessels. That constriction is why escharotomy rescues the limb.
